note: What is ORDINARY for a class of object, so that departure from it is the signal. This table is hand-authored data, not model output, and it is the only thing that decides whether a manoeuvre is unremarkable. Every figure is either derived from orbital mechanics here (with the derivation written out, so it can be checked) or taken from a published source (with a URL). Nothing in this file is an estimate someone remembered. Matching is by properties of ONE object -- its own catalog type, its own name, its own altitude, its own inclination, its own nodal rate. No entry compares two objects; see docs/mission-speculation-design.md section 1.6.
specificityNote: Higher `specificity` wins when several entries match. 0 is the regime default, 10 is a named constellation, 20 is a single named object.

deltaVBudgets.label: Geostationary north-south station-keeping
deltaVBudgets.derivation: Solar and lunar gravity torque the orbit plane of a geostationary satellite away from the equator at roughly 0.75 to 0.95 deg/yr, the rate varying over the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle. Rotating the plane back costs dv = 2 V sin(di/2) with V = sqrt(mu/a) = 3074.7 m/s at a = 42164 km. At 0.75 deg/yr that is 40.25 m/s/yr; at 0.85, 45.61; at 0.95, 50.98.
deltaVBudgets.teaching: This is the expensive half of holding a geostationary slot, and it is the reason a satellite's usable life is usually set by propellant rather than by electronics. Operators sometimes stop north-south keeping near end of life and let inclination grow, which is what an inclined-orbit lease is.

published.figure: 50 m/s per year, and about 95 per cent of a geostationary satellite's station-keeping propellant

sources.quote: The variation of velocity is 50 m.s-1 (North-South) and 5 m.s-1 (East-West) per year.
sources.cite: Dundeck et al., IOP Conf. Ser. Mater. Sci. Eng. 29 012010 (2012)

sources.quote: North-south station-keeping maneuvers about once every two weeks, with an annual delta v of about 50 meters per second, which represents 95% of the total station-keeping propellant budget.

published.agreement: The derivation above gives 40 to 51 m/s/yr from the luni-solar drift rate alone, and the published figure is 50. Two independent routes to the same number is the strongest form this table can take.

deltaVBudgets.label: Geostationary east-west station-keeping
deltaVBudgets.figure: about 2 m/s per year, in burns of a few cm/s every one to four weeks
deltaVBudgets.derivation: The Earth's equatorial ellipticity (the J22 term) gives the geostationary ring two stable longitudes near 75.1E and 104.9W and two unstable ones. A satellite away from a stable point accelerates in longitude at up to about 0.0018 deg/day^2, and holding a deadband of +/-0.05 to 0.1 deg against it costs of order 2 m/s per year. A single correction inside that deadband is a few centimetres per second, which changes the semi-major axis by of order a kilometre.
deltaVBudgets.teaching: East-west keeping is cheap because it is an in-plane change; north-south is expensive because it is a plane change. The same satellite pays both, and the ratio between them is about 25 to 1.

published.figure: between 2 and 5 m/s per year, corrections roughly weekly

sources.quote: East-west station-keeping maneuvers about once a week, with an annual delta v of less than 2 meters per second, to keep the satellite within 0.05 degrees of its assigned longitude.
The variation of velocity is 50 m.s-1 (North-South) and 5 m.s-1 (East-West) per year.

published.conflict: The two published figures disagree: under 2 m/s/yr against 5 m/s/yr. The range is shown rather than a choice being made. Either way the ratio to north-south keeping is between ten and twenty-five to one, which is the point worth teaching, and the derivation above lands inside the range.

deltaVBudgets.label: Geostationary end-of-life disposal raise
deltaVBudgets.figure: 8.5 to 11 m/s for a 235 to 300 km raise
deltaVBudgets.derivation: A two-burn transfer from a = 42164 km to a = 42399 km (a 235 km raise) costs 8.53 m/s; to 42464 km (300 km), 10.88 m/s. The IADC disposal guideline asks for a perigee at least 235 km above the geostationary ring plus a term proportional to the solar-radiation-pressure area-to-mass ratio, so the required raise is object-dependent and 235 km is the floor.
deltaVBudgets.teaching: Disposal costs about three months of north-south keeping. That is the trade an operator makes at end of life, and it is why a satellite that is abandoned in the ring rather than raised is a lasting hazard.

published.figure: 11 m/s for a 300 km raise, about three months of station-keeping propellant

sources.quote: The change in velocity that is required to raise the orbit altitude by 300 km is 11 meter/sec, and the required propellant corresponds to that necessary for three months of station keeping.
235 km is the sum of the upper altitude of the GEO protected region (200 km) and the maximum descent of a re-orbited spacecraft due to luni-solar and geopotential perturbations (35 km).
sources.cite: IADC-02-01 Rev.2, section 5.3.1; the required height is 235 + 1000*Cr*(A/M) km with e < 0.003, also ITU-R S.1003-2

published.agreement: The derivation above gives 10.88 m/s for a 300 km raise against ESA's published 11.

deltaVBudgets.label: Why inclination changes are the loud signal in low Earth orbit
deltaVBudgets.figure: at 550 km, 1 degree of plane change costs 132.4 m/s, while raising the orbit by 1 km costs 0.547 m/s
deltaVBudgets.derivation: At a = 6928 km the circular speed is 7585 m/s. A plane rotation costs dv = 2 V sin(di/2) = 132.4 m/s per degree. A tangential raise costs dv = n da / 2 with n = sqrt(mu/a^3), which is 0.547 m/s per km. The ratio is 242 to 1.
deltaVBudgets.teaching: This is the single most useful number for reading an orbital history. Maintenance is in-plane and cheap; a plane change is a decision. An operator who spends 130 m/s to move one degree has changed what the spacecraft is for, not merely kept it where it was.

deltaVBudgets.label: Low Earth orbit drag make-up, and how much the solar cycle changes it
deltaVBudgets.figure: 0.089 m/s/yr at solar minimum rising to 1.75 m/s/yr at solar maximum, at about 786 km -- a factor of nearly twenty, at a fixed altitude, for a fixed spacecraft

sources.cite: ESA, Guidelines for the computation of Delta-V and propellant budget, EOP-PhiMP/2019-07-2155, 11 November 2019
sources.quote: Annual drag compensation for a 730 kg spacecraft with Cd 3 and 4.5 m2 area at about 786 km, 2029 to 2038: 0.107, 0.089, 0.103, 0.335, 1.020, 1.747, 1.644, 1.241, 0.631, 0.283 m/s per year.

deltaVBudgets.teaching: This is the single best number on the page for connecting space weather to operations. Nothing about the satellite changes across that table -- same mass, same area, same altitude. The atmosphere it is flying through changes, because the Sun changed, and the propellant bill moves by a factor of twenty. It is also the reason NASA widened the ISS altitude band in March 2025: the old one was, in their words, difficult to maintain with monthly reboosts during solar maximum.

deltaVBudgets.label: Crewed station reboost at about 410 km
deltaVBudgets.figure: 0.24 to 2.3 m/s per burn, roughly monthly, so of order 12 m/s per year

sources.cite: NASA Glenn PIMS ISS Handbook, one document per reboost since 2010
sources.quote: Each reboost document states the GMT ignition time, the burn duration, the delta-v and the altitude change, giving both the planned value and the value derived independently from the SAMS accelerometers.

deltaVBudgets.teaching: Compare against the ESA figure above: the same physics at 410 km instead of 786 km, and the same spacecraft area-to-mass ratio to within twenty per cent, costs about ten times as much per year. The difference is entirely altitude, because neutral density falls roughly exponentially with a scale height of tens of kilometres.

citations.text: space-track's OBJECT_TYPE of DEBRIS denotes a fragment, not a spacecraft. It has no propulsion by definition, so any propulsive signature on it is a false alarm.

A catalogued ROCKET BODY is a spent upper stage. Some stages perform a disposal burn shortly after separation, but a stage that has been catalogued and tracked for more than a few days is inert. Treated here as unable to manoeuvre, which is the conservative direction for a false-alarm control: any real late disposal burn inflates the measured false-alarm rate rather than hiding it.

A low Earth orbit payload maintains its altitude against drag with small in-plane burns. The ceiling of 25 m/s per event is set so that anything larger is flagged for a reader's attention: at 550 km, 25 m/s is a 46 km altitude change or a fifth of a degree of plane change, both of which are campaigns rather than maintenance.

A sun-synchronous orbit's whole value is that its J2 nodal regression equals the mean sun's apparent motion, +0.9856 deg/day, which fixes the local solar time of every pass. That rate depends on both altitude and inclination, so an operator holding the local time constant must adjust BOTH -- small inclination corrections are ordinary maintenance for this class, and only for this class. Elsewhere an inclination change is a mission change.

Starlink spacecraft use krypton or argon Hall-effect thrusters, which are low-thrust and electric: a manoeuvre is spread over many revolutions rather than delivered impulsively, so it appears in the elements as a sustained trend rather than a step. Objects in this fleet are also routinely raising from an injection orbit, holding an operational shell, or being lowered for disposal at any given moment, so almost every in-plane signature is ordinary for them and the interesting question is the SIZE, not the fact.

OneWeb flies a near-polar shell at about 1,200 km, where atmospheric drag is negligible on the timescale of an element set. Station-keeping there is about holding a slot within the constellation's own geometry, not about fighting the atmosphere, so corrections are very small -- of order a centimetre per second -- and a raise of even tens of metres in semi-major axis is a real, deliberate act.

A navigation constellation at about 20,000 km sees no meaningful drag and only slow luni-solar plane drift, and its orbits are chosen so the ground track repeats. Station-keeping is therefore infrequent and small, and its purpose is to hold the repeat -- which is a property of the semi-major axis, so the corrections are in-plane.

A crewed station in low Earth orbit loses altitude continuously and is reboosted by a visiting vehicle. Reboosts are large enough to be unmistakable in the elements, are announced in advance, and are the best-documented manoeuvres in orbit -- which is why this class is the anchor of the positive control in data/orbit_manoeuvre_truth.json.

Measured across forty published ISS reboosts from 2020 to 2026, the per-event delta-v runs from 0.24 to 2.3 m/s. The ceiling of 3.0 m/s here is set just above the largest one NASA has published, so a larger burn is flagged for a reader rather than passed over.
